top_evidence.document_title: Endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection for colorectal laterally spreading tumors (> 20 mm): a systematic review and meta-analysis
top_evidence.text: The reporting of this systematic review follows the recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (Supplementary Material 1) [10]. Quality assessment: Search strategy: The risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers (Q.Z. and T.K.) using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB 2) for randomized trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for nonrandomized controlled studies. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or by consulting a third reviewer (T.Z.). An electronic literature search was conducted by an experienced librarian with supervision from the study's principal investigator. Multiple databases were searched from inception to 1 May 2025, to identify eligible studies. The databases searched included PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane. The search strategies employed in PubMed and Cochrane Library databases were as follows: (((colorectal tumors) OR (laterally spreading tumor)) AND (endoscopic submucosal dissection) OR (ESD)) AND ((piecemeal endoscopic mucosal resection) OR (pEMR) OR (piecemeal EMR) OR (pmEMR) OR (EMR-precutting) OR (EMR-P) OR (endoscopic piecemeal mucosal resection) OR(EPMR)). The search strategy applied in the Embase database was: (colorectal AND ('tumors'/exp OR tumors) OR laterally) AND spreading AND ('tumor'/exp OR tumor) AND (endoscopic AND submucosal AND ('dissection'/exp OR dissection) OR esd) AND (((piecemeal AND endoscopic AND mucosal AND ('resection'/exp OR resection) OR pemr OR piecemeal) AND emr OR pmemr OR 'emr precutting' OR 'emr p' OR endoscopic) AND piecemeal AND mucosal AND ('resection'/exp OR resection) OR epmr).

top_evidence.section: Results > Statistical Analysis > Search Results And Population Characteristics
top_evidence.text: Statistical analyses were performed using the Cochrane Collaboration's RevMan 5.4 software. Statistical analyses were performed using the Cochrane Collaboration's RevMan 5.4 software. Data were analyzed using randomeffects models, with forest plots generated for each outcome. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Heterogeneity was assessed via Q -test and I 2 statistics. Sensitivity analysis employed the leave-one-out method to evaluate robustness. Publication bias was initially evaluated through funnel plot visualization and confirmed with Egger's test (Stata 18.0). Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05 (heterogeneity threshold: p < 0.1). A total of 111 duplicate records were excluded using EndNote. After removing reviews, meta-analyses, letters, editorials, case reports/series, and ineligible publications, eight studies were ultimately included (see PRISMA flowchart, Fig. 1). The analysis comprised 3024 patients: 1451 underwent ESD and 1573 received EMR (including 588 piecemeal EMR procedures). Included studies consisted of one RCT and seven retrospective studies (six single-center, two multicenter), with geographical distribution as follows: three from South Korea, three from Japan, one from Germany, and one from France. Detailed study characteristics are summarized in Table 1. We used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for nonrandomized studies to assess methodology quality, which gave a mean score of 7.7 (range 6-9) (Table 2) [18]. For the randomized trials, we used Cochrane's Risk of Bias assessment (Table 3) [19]. General characteristics of the studies and characteristics of the included lesions were shown in Table 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection for colorectal laterally spreading tumors (> 20 mm): a systematic review and meta-analysis
top_evidence.text: to rise in recent years, particularly in developing countries. This high incidence and mortality underscore the critical importance of early detection and intervention. Laterally spreading tumors (LSTs) have been recognized as important precursors of CRC [2]. In 2020, colorectal cancer (CRC) accounted for over 1.9 million new cases and approximately 0.9 million deaths globally, making it the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide [1]. The incidence of CRC has continued T. Zhang 305514271@qq.com Q. Zeng 2027863081@qq.com L. Zhang 286535795@qq.com T. Kong 424201342@qq.com S. Xu C. Lan 369911243@qq.com B. He hbb1987@qq.com * 1 Department of Gastroenterology, The Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University, Nanchong Central Hospital, Luzhou 646000, Sichuan, China 2 Nanchong Central Hospital, Nanchong 637000, China 2026682455@qq.com LSTs are defined as flat, broad-based lesions with a minimum diameter of 10 mm, predominantly located in the colorectum. Based on endoscopic morphology, LSTs are classified into two subtypes: granular type (LST-G) and nongranular type (LST-NG) [3]. These lesions have the potential to progress to high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia, with incidence rates reported up to 33.8% [4, 5]. Therefore, the early identification and resection of colorectal LSTs are essential for the prevention and treatment of carcinogenesis. Study selection: Inclusion criteria: (1) Studies involving LSTs with lesions measuring > 20 mm; (2) Comparative studies reporting primary and secondary outcomes of ESD versus EMR. Exclusion criteria: (1) Studies including LSTs < 20 mm or other lesions preventing outcome extraction; (2) Reviews, meta-analyses, letters, editorials; (3) Case reports/series or studies with < 30 patients per ESD/EMR group; (4) Animal studies. Compared with surgical intervention, endoscopic treatment has been widely adopted owing to its minimally invasive nature, rapid recovery, and cost-effectiveness. The main endoscopic techniques for LSTs include endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) and endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR). For lesions larger than 20 mm, EMR often necessitates piecemeal resection (PEMR), whereas ESD enables en bloc resection [6]. Several studies have compared the efficacy and safety of ESD and EMR for large colorectal LSTs. However, for LSTs exceeding 20 mm in diameter, the optimal choice between ESD and EMR remains controversial [6-9]. To date, no systematic review or meta-analysis has specifically compared the efficacy and safety of ESD versus EMR for the resection of colorectal LSTs greater than 20 mm. Therefore, this systematic review aims to comprehensively evaluate the efficacy and safety of ESD and EMR for colorectal LSTs larger than 20 mm, providing evidencebased guidance for clinical decision-making. Two reviewers (initials, Q.Z. and L.Z.) independently screened the titles and abstracts of all records identified by the search. Full-text articles of potentially eligible studies were then independently assessed by the same two reviewers for eligibility. Disagreements at any stage were resolved through discussion or, if necessary, by consulting a third reviewer (T.Z.). The reasons for excluding studies at the fulltext stage were recorded. The selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1). Data extraction: Data were extracted independently by two reviewers (Q.Z. and T.K.) using a predefined data extraction form. The extracted data included: first author, publication year, study design (single-center/multicenter), total patients, EMR/ ESD techniques, recurrence, and adverse events (delayed bleeding, perforation). Any discrepancies in data extraction were resolved by consensus or by involving a third reviewer (S.X.). If necessary, study authors were contacted for clarification or additional data. The data extraction forms and analytic code are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

top_evidence.text: The GRADE working group approach was used to rate the quality of evidence. Based on the predominance of observational studies and negligible heterogeneity ( I 2 < 5%), the overall evidence was rated as low certainty. However, for local recurrence, the certainty was upgraded to moderate due to the very large magnitude of effect (OR 0.06).
